plan: Humanities argument passage (CLD-P-ACT-R-000008) on eighteenth-century sham ruins: objection-and-rebuttal structure, figurative language, examples-to-claim function; choice lengths kept even.

passages.title: Ruins on Purpose
passages.text:
In eighteenth-century England, a landowner who wanted his estate to look properly distinguished might commission, alongside the lawns and lakes, a ruin. Not an old building that had fallen down, but a new one designed to look as if it had: a broken tower with an artfully collapsed staircase, a chapel wall with empty windows framing a view of the hills. Builders were sometimes instructed to leave stones scattered at the base, as though they had dropped there over centuries.

To a modern visitor, the practice can seem faintly absurd, even dishonest. We are accustomed to valuing old buildings for their authenticity, for the fact that they were actually there when the events we associate with them took place. A ruin built in 1760 to evoke the Middle Ages appears to offer the feeling of history without the thing itself, the way a souvenir offers the feeling of a trip.

But that judgment assumes the builders were trying to deceive, and there is little evidence that they were. Visitors generally knew which ruins were new; guidebooks said so, and owners were often proud of the fact. What the sham ruin offered was not a false claim about the past but an occasion for a particular state of mind. Writers of the period described the pleasure of contemplating decay: the reminder that all human works, including the grand house a few hundred yards away, would eventually crumble. The ruin was less a history lesson than a kind of philosophical furniture.

Seen this way, the sham ruin tells us less about how the eighteenth century misunderstood the past than about how it used the past. History, for these landowners, was not primarily a record to be consulted but a mood to be cultivated, a backdrop against which the present could feel both important and fleeting. The broken tower did not need to be old to do its work. It needed only to be broken.

It is tempting to feel superior to this attitude, and in some ways we are right to. The modern preservation movement, with its insistence on original materials and documented histories, has saved a great deal that the eighteenth century would have let fall or would have cheerfully "improved." Yet the impulse behind the sham ruin has not disappeared. It survives whenever a new restaurant installs reclaimed barn wood, or a housing development is named for the farm it replaced. We still want the feeling of age; we have simply become more particular about where it comes from.

candidates.stem: The main purpose of the passage is to:

choices.A: argue that sham ruins deserve the same careful preservation as genuine old buildings.
choices.B: describe the building techniques used to make new structures look centuries old.
choices.C: reinterpret a practice that can seem dishonest by explaining what it was meant to do.
choices.D: criticize the modern preservation movement for valuing authenticity too highly.

candidates.evidence: But that judgment assumes the builders were trying to deceive, and there is little evidence that they were.
candidates.explanation: The passage raises the modern charge of dishonesty, rebuts it, and explains the ruins' purpose: an occasion for contemplating time and decay.

A.rationale: The passage never argues for preserving sham ruins.

B.rationale: Construction details appear only in paragraph 1 as setup.

D.rationale: The author says we are "right" in some ways and credits what preservation has saved.

hints: What does it say the ruins were for?

strategy.explanation: Summarize the argument in one sentence first.

candidates.remember: A purpose answer must cover the whole argument.

candidates.stem: According to the passage, builders of sham ruins were sometimes instructed to:

choices.A: leave stones scattered around the base of the structure.
choices.B: reuse stones taken from genuine medieval buildings nearby.
choices.C: place each ruin where it could be seen from the main road.
choices.D: copy the exact design of a particular medieval chapel.

candidates.evidence: Builders were sometimes instructed to leave stones scattered at the base
candidates.explanation: Paragraph 1 says builders were sometimes told to leave stones scattered at the base.

B.rationale: The passage never mentions reused medieval stone.

C.rationale: Placement relative to roads is not mentioned.

D.rationale: No specific chapel is said to have been copied.

hints: Look near the end of paragraph 1.
candidates.remember: Detail answers restate a specific line.

candidates.stem: The comparison to a souvenir in paragraph 2 primarily serves to:

choices.A: show that eighteenth-century visitors bought souvenirs when they toured ruins.
choices.B: illustrate a modern objection that the author then goes on to challenge.
choices.C: reveal that the author considers sham ruins to be essentially worthless.
choices.D: explain why landowners chose to build ruins near their own grand houses.

candidates.evidence: But that judgment assumes the builders were trying to deceive
candidates.explanation: Paragraph 2 voices the modern view that sham ruins offer only the feeling of history, like a souvenir; paragraph 3 calls this a "judgment" and challenges it.

A.rationale: The souvenir is an analogy, not a historical detail.

C.rationale: Paragraph 3 begins "But that judgment assumes," so the view is not the author's own.

D.rationale: The comparison concerns modern judgment, not landowners' reasons.

hints: How does paragraph 3 respond to it?

strategy.explanation: Check whether the author endorses or challenges the view.

candidates.remember: An author may present a view in order to dispute it.

candidates.stem: The author mentions that "guidebooks said so" (paragraph 3) mainly as evidence that:

choices.A: guidebooks were the main source of historical knowledge for visitors.
choices.B: visitors of the period preferred new ruins to genuinely old ones.
choices.C: owners were privately embarrassed by the ruins they had built.
choices.D: the builders were not trying to fool visitors about the ruins' age.

candidates.evidence: there is little evidence that they were. Visitors generally knew which ruins were new; guidebooks said so
candidates.explanation: The author claims there is little evidence of deception; guidebooks openly identifying new ruins supports that claim.

A.rationale: The point is what the guidebooks reveal about honesty, not their role in education.

B.rationale: Nothing compares visitors' preferences for new and old ruins.

C.rationale: Owners were "often proud of the fact."

hints: What claim comes just before this evidence?

strategy.explanation: Link the evidence to the claim it supports.

candidates.remember: Ask which claim a piece of evidence supports.

candidates.subskill: Meaning of a word in context
candidates.stem: As it is used in paragraph 3, the word "occasion" most nearly means:
candidates.evidence: What the sham ruin offered was not a false claim about the past but an occasion for a particular state of mind.
candidates.explanation: The ruin provided a chance, or opening, for a certain mood: an "opportunity."

C.rationale: An excuse justifies something; the ruin invites a state of mind.

hints: Substitute each choice into the sentence.
candidates.remember: Common words often carry less common meanings in context.

candidates.stem: The phrase "philosophical furniture" (paragraph 3) suggests that the author sees sham ruins primarily as:

choices.A: objects that furnished a setting for reflection on time and decay.
choices.B: practical structures that owners used to store household goods.
choices.C: decorative imitations of fashionable furniture styles of the period.
choices.D: displays meant chiefly to advertise their owners' great wealth.

candidates.evidence: Writers of the period described the pleasure of contemplating decay
candidates.explanation: The phrase concludes a description of the pleasure of contemplating decay, so the ruins are seen as props that equip a landscape for philosophical thought.

B.rationale: "Furniture" is figurative; no practical use is mentioned.

C.rationale: The phrase is a metaphor, not a reference to actual furniture design.

D.rationale: Paragraph 1 mentions looking distinguished, but the phrase follows a description of contemplating decay.

hints: What does the sentence before the phrase describe?

strategy.explanation: Read the phrase together with the sentence before it.

candidates.remember: Interpret a metaphor through its immediate context.

candidates.stem: Based on paragraph 4, the author would most likely say that a sham ruin succeeded if it:

choices.A: convinced visitors that it had truly been built in the Middle Ages.
choices.B: taught visitors accurate facts about the history of their region.
choices.C: led visitors to reflect on time and the impermanence of their world.
choices.D: matched the architectural style of the main house on the estate.

candidates.evidence: a backdrop against which the present could feel both important and fleeting
candidates.explanation: Paragraph 4 says the ruin's work was to create a mood in which the present felt important and fleeting; it "needed only to be broken."

A.rationale: Paragraph 3 says visitors generally knew the ruins were new.

B.rationale: History was "not primarily a record to be consulted."

D.rationale: Matching styles is never mentioned as a goal.

hints: What was the ruin's "work," according to paragraph 4?

strategy.explanation: Eliminate goals the author says the ruins did not have.

candidates.remember: Apply the author's own stated criterion.

candidates.stem: In the last paragraph, the author's attitude toward the modern preservation movement is best described as:

choices.A: approving of what it has saved, while noting that the wish for a feeling of age persists.
choices.B: dismissive, because it values original materials more than the moods buildings create.
choices.C: nostalgic for the period before the movement existed, when ruins were built freely.
choices.D: neutral, since the author describes the movement without evaluating it in any way.

candidates.evidence: has saved a great deal that the eighteenth century would have let fall
candidates.explanation: The author grants that we are right in some ways and that preservation has saved much, then adds that the desire for the feeling of age has not disappeared.

B.rationale: The author credits it with saving a great deal.

C.rationale: The author never expresses longing for that period.

D.rationale: "In some ways we are right to" feel superior is an evaluation.

hints: What does the author credit the movement with?

strategy.explanation: Eliminate attitudes that are too extreme or too flat.

candidates.remember: Mixed attitudes often pair a concession with a "yet."

candidates.stem: The examples of reclaimed barn wood and a housing development named for a farm (paragraph 5) mainly serve to:

choices.A: illustrate the preservation movement's insistence on using original materials.
choices.B: show that a modern version of the sham ruin's appeal still exists today.
choices.C: criticize modern builders for deliberately deceiving their customers.
choices.D: explain the reasons that eighteenth-century landowners built ruins.

candidates.evidence: Yet the impulse behind the sham ruin has not disappeared. It survives whenever
candidates.explanation: The examples follow the claim that the impulse "has not disappeared" and show new places borrowing the feeling of age.

A.rationale: Reclaimed wood here supplies a feeling of age to a new building, not preservation of an old one.

C.rationale: The author does not accuse anyone of deception; the point is a shared desire.

D.rationale: The examples are modern, not explanations of past motives.

hints: What claim do the examples follow?

strategy.explanation: Read the sentence right before the examples.

candidates.remember: Examples support the claim just before them.

candidates.stem: Which choice best describes the structure of the passage's argument?

choices.A: It traces the history of ruins in England from the Middle Ages to modern times.
choices.B: It compares two rival theories of why ruins were built and then endorses one of them.
choices.C: It describes a practice, states an objection, rebuts it, and links the practice to the present.
choices.D: It argues that modern preservation is misguided and proposes a better alternative.

candidates.evidence: It is tempting to feel superior to this attitude
candidates.explanation: Paragraph 1 describes sham ruins; paragraph 2 gives the modern objection; paragraphs 3 and 4 rebut it; paragraph 5 connects the impulse to the present.

A.rationale: The passage focuses on eighteenth-century sham ruins, not a full history.

B.rationale: Only one objection and one interpretation are presented.

D.rationale: The author largely approves of modern preservation.

strategy.explanation: Outline the paragraphs before reading the choices.

candidates.remember: Structure answers must fit every paragraph in order.
